title: The song in The Princess
short: A song from The Princess (1847), Part IV, sung by one of Princess Ida's maids; it was not, as the archive heading suggests, first printed in 1895.
body: The lyric appeared in the first edition of The Princess: A Medley (1847), a long narrative poem about a princess who founds a university for women. In Part IV a maid sings it among Ida's party; Ida answers by dismissing such backward-looking feeling and urging that the past be let go in favour of the future. Tennyson said the song came to him in autumn at Tintern Abbey, a place 'full for me of its bygone memories' (Memoir I, 253). Read in context, the song is a dramatic utterance whose melancholy is challenged; read alone, as it nearly always is, it becomes one of the purest lyrics of loss in English. Hill's 1971 anthology of Tennyson describes it as among his most Virgilian poems.

anchor: I know not what they mean
title: Why the tears? 'the passion of the past'
short: The speaker weeps without knowing why; Tennyson called the feeling 'the passion of the past', and critics dispute whether the cause is personal or general.
body: Tennyson told James Knowles that the poem expressed a lifelong sense he called 'the passion of the past', the abiding in the transient. Cleanth Brooks, in a famous New Critical reading, argued that the poem dramatises the paradox of tears that are 'idle' (purposeless) yet spring from a 'divine' source, and that the speaker discovers their meaning as the poem proceeds. Graham Hough answered that the grief is deliberately undifferentiated, which also explains the absence of rhyme. Biographical critics have related the sorrow to Hallam's death (he was buried not far across the Severn at Clevedon) or, for the last stanza, to Rosa Baring, but the poem itself refuses a specific cause.

title: idle
short: Useless, without cause or result; the tears seem to serve no purpose and answer no present grief.
body: The older senses of 'idle' (OED) include 'empty, vain, worthless' and 'without ground or foundation', as in 'idle words'. The tears are idle because nothing in the present scene, the 'happy Autumn-fields', explains them, and because weeping cannot recover what is lost. Brooks made the word central to his reading: the poem's task is to show that tears called idle in the first line are in fact deeply motivated, so that the adjective is ironically undone by what follows.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'idle, adj.'

title: divine despair
greek: Latin divinus; de- + sperare, to be without hope
short: An oxymoron: despair was theologically a sin, yet this despair seems to come from a source beyond the self.
body: In Christian tradition despair, the loss of hope in God's mercy, is a grave sin, so 'divine despair' is a striking paradox. Readers have taken 'divine' to mean 'god-like, exalted', 'mysterious in origin', or 'springing from the soul's divine part', a longing that no earthly object can satisfy. Brooks treats the phrase as the first of the poem's paradoxes, holding together purposelessness and profundity. The tears 'rise' from 'the depth', an image of a spring welling upward, which anticipates the vertical images of ships rising and sinking in stanza 2.

title: the happy Autumn-fields
short: Harvest fields, 'happy' because fruitful; the season of fulfilment prompts not joy but a sense of time's passing.
body: 'Happy' carries its older sense of 'fortunate, prosperous' (compare Latin felix, used of fertile land). Autumn traditionally marks both fruition and decline, so the harvest scene holds together completeness and ending. Tennyson associated the song with an autumn visit to Tintern Abbey, the ruined Cistercian house in the Wye valley that Wordsworth had made a site of memory in 'Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey' (1798); critics compare the two poems' treatment of revisiting the past, Wordsworth's consoling, Tennyson's mournful.

anchor: the days that are no more
title: Refrain and unrhymed stanzas
short: Each of the four five-line stanzas of blank verse closes on the same phrase, which supplies the binding role normally given to rhyme.
body: The poem is in unrhymed iambic pentameter, divided into four five-line stanzas; the closing phrase 'the days that are no more' acts as a refrain. Most of the songs in The Princess rhyme (though 'Now sleeps the crimson petal' and 'Come down, O maid' do not), and Hough asked why this one is unrhymed, arguing that rhyme would give too definite a shape to an indefinite grief. The refrain is varied by what precedes it: 'So sad, so fresh', 'So sad, so strange', and finally 'O Death in Life', so that a fixed phrase gathers new meaning. The phrase 'no more' was a favourite Tennysonian cadence of finality.

title: Fresh ... Sad: the ship simile
short: The past is both fresh, like a ship bringing friends home at dawn, and sad, like a ship sinking with loved ones below the horizon.
body: Stanza 2 is built on a double simile. The first light catches the sail of a ship coming in, bringing friends back; the last light of sunset reddens over a ship that disappears over the horizon, carrying away 'all we love'. Memory is simultaneously vivid (fresh) and grievous (sad), because what it presents so vividly is gone. Brooks noted that the images are of arrivals and departures, of the past as both returning and receding. The pairing of 'first' and 'last' beams frames the stanza within a single day.

sources.cite: Cleanth Brooks, 'The Motivation of Tennyson's Weeper', in The Well Wrought Urn (New York, 1947)

title: underworld
short: Here primarily the other side of the earth, below the horizon from which the ship rises; the sense of the realm of the dead is also present.
body: The OED records an older sense of 'underworld' as the region below the horizon or the antipodes, as well as the classical abode of the dead (Hades). Literally the ship climbs into view from beyond the curve of the earth. Yet the word inevitably suggests that the returning friends come back from death, which gives the line its poignancy: the image of reunion is shadowed by the impossibility of the dead returning. Editors gloss both senses; the doubleness is characteristic of the poem's method.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'underworld, n.'

title: verge
short: The horizon, the edge of the visible sea; the ship 'sinks' out of sight as the sun sets.
body: 'Verge' means the edge or rim of something (OED), and was used poetically of the horizon. 'Sinks' describes a ship disappearing over the horizon, but it also suggests drowning, and 'all we love' turns the image towards death. Readers have connected the image with the ship that brought Hallam's body home from Trieste, which Tennyson mourns elsewhere (compare In Memoriam IX, 'Fair ship, that from the Italian shore').

title: The deathbed dawn
short: A dying person hears the first birdsong and sees the window grow pale at dawn: the familiar world becomes strange because it will be lost.
body: The third stanza moves from sea to sickroom. In the dark of a summer dawn the first 'pipe' (piping song) of birds not yet fully awake reaches someone who will not see the day out. 'Strange' is the key word: the ordinary becomes unfamiliar because it is perceived for the last time. The speaker's relation to the past is thus likened to the dying person's relation to the present, sharpening the idea that the past is a kind of death within life, which the last line will name. Brooks admired the precision of the visual detail that follows.

sources.cite: Cleanth Brooks, 'The Motivation of Tennyson's Weeper', in The Well Wrought Urn (New York, 1947)

title: casement
short: A hinged window; to failing eyes in the half-dark, its outline slowly emerges as a faintly shining square of light.
body: A casement is a window that opens on hinges (OED). The line records exactly how a window appears before sunrise in a dark room: not as a view but as a pale, glimmering shape. The verb 'grows' makes the light seem to develop slowly, matching the slow fading of the dying eyes. The monosyllabic, heavily stressed line enacts slowness. The image is frequently praised as an instance of Tennyson's exact observation used for emotional effect.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'casement, n.'

title: hopeless fancy feigned / On lips that are for others
short: Kisses only imagined on the lips of someone who belongs to another: unrequited or forbidden love.
body: The final stanza compares the past to two kinds of kisses: those remembered after a loved one's death, and those merely imagined ('feigned', invented) by a lover without hope, on lips 'that are for others', that is, promised to someone else. 'Fancy' here means imagination, with a suggestion of love-fancy. Biographical critics, following Ralph Rader's work on Maud, have connected the lines with Tennyson's disappointed attachment to Rosa Baring in the mid-1830s; others caution against reducing the poem's deliberately universal grief to a single episode.

title: O Death in Life
short: The past is a death carried within the living present; the phrase inverts Coleridge's spectre 'Life-in-Death' in The Ancient Mariner.
body: The final refrain replaces 'so sad, so strange' with an apostrophe: the days that are no more are 'Death in Life', a death experienced while living. Coleridge's Ancient Mariner (Part III) personifies 'The Night-mare LIFE-IN-DEATH', a condition of living on in suffering; Tennyson's reversal makes memory a presence of death within life. The phrase gathers the poem's paradoxes (idle/divine, fresh/sad, dear/deep) into one, and is often read as Tennyson's summary of the elegiac mood shared by In Memoriam and 'Tithonus'.

title: Virgilian tears
short: Critics call the poem Virgilian: like Aeneas weeping at Carthage, the speaker is moved by the tears inherent in mortal things.
body: In Aeneid 1.462 Aeneas, seeing the Trojan War depicted on the walls of Juno's temple at Carthage, says 'sunt lacrimae rerum et mentem mortalia tangunt' ('there are tears for things, and mortal matters touch the mind'). Tennyson revered Virgil (see his ode 'To Virgil', 1882, which hails the Roman poet as majestic in his sadness at human fate), and the description of the song as among his most Virgilian poems rests on this shared sense of a sorrow belonging to existence rather than to one event. The line itself traces the physical movement of tears from 'heart' to 'eyes', unifying feeling and body.
